newsitem.title: CHINA: Tibet share seen a hit despite uncertain future.
newsitem.headline: Tibet share seen a hit despite uncertain future.

text.p: The first industrial share to be issued by a Tibetan company will be a success despite an uncertain future for its main product, mineral water, brokers said on Monday.
Tibet Shendi Corp said on Monday it plans to raise 57 million yuan ($6.87 million) when it issues 15 million A shares this week on the Shanghai stock exchange.
The company runs a hotel and tourism company, and produces "Himalayan," "Holy Land" and "Potala" brand mineral water in the regional capital of Lhasa.
It is also planing to build Tibet's biggest commercial complex with part of the money raised from the issue, it said in a statement in the Shanghai Securities News.
"If this company were in Shanghai or Guangdong, it would not be able to list," said an analyst with a Western brokerage. "It does not have the scale, turnover or level of profits."
"But the issue will go well because we are in a bull market, the price of each share is low, and the total issue volume is low," he said. "Everyone will be happy -- Beijing, Tibet and the investors."
"The most important reason for the listing is that, like other parts of China, Tibet has a quota for listing," one Chinese broker said.

"This quota system is part of the old state planning system," he said. To ensure that not all the listed companies come from the richest areas of China, Beijing has distributed a share quota to all provinces and regions of the country.
Competition among companies to list shares in China is fierce, especially during a bull market such as the one that began in April this year, in Shanghai and Shenzhen.
Compared to the industrial giants of east China, Tibet Shendi is a minnow, as befits China's poorest region.
In the first half of 1996 it posted net profit of 1.922 million yuan on turnover of 9.75 million, against net profit of 1.562 million on turnover of 14.45 million in all 1995.
It plans to earn 50 percent of its future revenue from sales of mineral water, but production only began last October.
The mineral water has to be taken by truck more than 1,000 km (625 miles) over the Tibetan plateau to Golmud, from where it is taken by train to the main cities of China.
Of the other half of its future revenue, 30 percent will come from its hotel and tourism business and 20 percent from the commercial complex, the statement said.
The analyst said he was worried about this dependence on mineral water. Competition is fierce in China's mineral water market and profit margins are low.

"I am more confident about the development of the tourism industry in Tibet, especially domestic visitors." he said. "It is increasingly fashionable to go to inland places like Tibet, and the price of going there is not considered excessive."
Tibet attracted 100,000 visitors in 1995 and the number is growing at 20 percent a year. The company's Himalaya Hotel ranks fifth in Tibet in terms of visitors, the company said.
Hotel group Tibet Pearl Star Co listed A shares in Shanghai in February 1995. But nearly all its assets are not in Tibet but in the neighbouring province of Sichuan.
